name: Karim's
description: The century-old Mughlai institution in Gali Kababian, run by descendants of cooks who claim a lineage to the Mughal kitchens. Smoky seekh kebabs, mutton burra and a korma that has converted generations of Delhiites. Cramped, chaotic, unbeatable.
editor_note: Skip the butter chicken everywhere else and order the mutton burra with khameeri roti here instead.

name: Al Jawahar
description: Karim's quieter neighbour by Jama Masjid Gate No. 1, and many locals' actual pick of the two. The nihari at breakfast and the mutton korma are the moves, eaten under whirring fans with tandoor smoke drifting in from the front.
editor_note: Come before 10am for the nihari - it sells out, and that is not a marketing line.

name: Paranthe Wali Gali
description: A narrow Chandni Chowk lane where a handful of shops, some running since the 1870s, fry stuffed parathas in kadhais of ghee. Fillings run from classic aloo to rabri and papad, all served with the same set of sweet-and-sour chutneys.
editor_note: Pt. Gaya Prasad Shiv Charan is the one with the family tree on the wall - order the mixed plate and split it.

name: Natraj Dahi Bhalla Corner
description: A tiny 1940s counter near the Chandni Chowk metro that sells exactly two things: dahi bhalla and aloo tikki. Both arrive drowned in cold sweet curd and tamarind chutney, and both have queues that move with assembly-line speed.
editor_note: There is no seating and there never will be - eat standing in the lane like everyone has since 1940.

name: Old Famous Jalebi Wala
description: On the Dariba Kalan corner since 1884, frying thick, desi-ghee jalebis in enormous iron kadhais. These are not the wiry jalebis of sweet shops elsewhere - they are fat, syrup-heavy coils sold hot by the kilo.
editor_note: Ask for them taza, straight from the kadhai, and eat them walking into Dariba Kalan's silver lane.

name: Kuremal Mohan Lal Kulfi Wale
description: A Sitaram Bazar legend famous for stuffed-fruit kulfi - whole mangoes, pomegranates and oranges hollowed out, filled with kulfi and frozen. The fruit-cream flavours rotate with the season and taste like nothing made in a factory.
editor_note: Get the stuffed mango kulfi in summer and let them slice it like a fruit at the counter.

name: Jama Masjid at Sunrise
description: Shah Jahan's great mosque is at its best just after dawn, when the red sandstone courtyard is nearly empty and pigeons wheel over the minarets. Climb the southern minaret for a rooftop view of the old city waking up.
editor_note: Go at first light, before the tour groups, then walk straight to Al Jawahar for nihari.

name: Daryaganj Sunday Book Market (Mahila Haat)
description: The legendary Sunday second-hand book bazaar, now relocated into Mahila Haat but still the same sprawl of sellers with everything from pulp thrillers to out-of-print Penguin classics on tarpaulins. Books by the piece or, at some stalls, by the kilo.
editor_note: Carry cash, go before noon, and haggle gently - the good first editions vanish by lunchtime.

name: Khari Baoli Spice Market
description: Asia's largest wholesale spice market, running since the 17th century - sacks of dried chillies, nuts, pickles and teas stacked to the ceilings, with porters threading through clouds of pepper dust that will make you sneeze. Climb the stairs inside Gadodia Market for the rooftop view over Fatehpuri Masjid.
editor_note: The unmarked staircase in Gadodia Market leads to a rooftop panorama most visitors never find.

name: Kake Di Hatti
description: A 1942 dhaba near Fatehpuri Masjid serving naans the size of car tyres, stuffed with paneer, gobhi or keema-style soya, with dal makhani that simmers all day. Portions are built for sharing and the kitchen runs deep into the night.
editor_note: One stuffed naan feeds two people comfortably - order accordingly or be defeated.

name: Haji Mohd. Hussain Fried Chicken
description: Matia Mahal's answer to fried chicken everywhere else: birds marinated in a closely guarded masala and flash-fried in bubbling oil at the shopfront. Crisp, turmeric-stained and served with rumali roti and chutney on steel plates.
editor_note: Go after dark during Ramzan if you can - the whole lane turns into a festival around it.

name: Lala Babu Chaat Bhandar
description: A Chandni Chowk chaat counter where the kalmi vada and pao-style tikki have been drawing crowds for decades. Everything is assembled to order with a flick-of-the-wrist speed that is half the entertainment.
editor_note: The kalmi vada chaat is the sleeper hit - most first-timers wrongly default to the tikki.

name: Pandit Ved Prakash Lemon Wale
description: A century-old soda stall opposite Town Hall selling banta - lemon soda in marble-stoppered bottles - spiked with masala, kala namak and lime. The pop of the marble and the first salty-fizzy sip is pure Chandni Chowk summer.
editor_note: Order it kacha-nimbu style with extra masala and drink it fast before the fizz dies.

name: Giani's Di Hatti
description: The 1951 original near Fatehpuri Masjid that spawned the Giani's ice-cream chain, still best for what it started with: rabri faluda and hot gajar halwa in winter. The rabri is thick enough to fight your spoon.
editor_note: Winter rule of the old city: hot halwa first, faluda after, never the other way around.

name: Indian Coffee House
description: The worker-cooperative coffee house atop Mohan Singh Place, frozen somewhere in 1975 - turbaned waiters, sticky formica tables, filter coffee and mutton dosas for pocket change. Once the adda of journalists and revolutionaries; the terrace still catches the CP breeze.
editor_note: Order the cold coffee and a scrambled-egg toast, take the terrace seats, and stay all afternoon - nobody will hurry you.

name: Triveni Terrace Cafe
description: Tucked into the Triveni Kala Sangam arts complex near Mandi House, an open terrace cafe overlooking an amphitheatre and frangipani trees. Simple, honest thalis, keema pao and nimbu pani for the theatre-and-gallery crowd.
editor_note: Catch an exhibition downstairs, then get the mutton curry-chawal before the lunch rush of rehearsing actors arrives.

name: Oxford Bookstore
description: The grand old bookstore chain's Delhi flagship in Statesman House, with a serious India shelf, a children's corner and the Cha Bar attached - a tea menu running to over a hundred brews. Browsing here is an afternoon, not an errand.
editor_note: Buy your book, then claim a Cha Bar window seat with a pot of first-flush Darjeeling.

name: Agrasen ki Baoli
description: A 14th-century stepwell hidden between office towers off Hailey Road - 108 stone steps descending into cool, pigeon-haunted silence a minute from the CP roar. Equal parts architecture lesson and city escape hatch.
editor_note: Go at opening time on a weekday and you might have all 108 steps to yourself.

name: Wenger's
description: CP's Swiss-founded bakery, open since 1926 and still mobbed at all hours for shammi kebab patties, chicken croissants and rum balls handed over the marble counter. There is nowhere to sit; you eat on the colonnade like everyone else.
editor_note: The veg patties and a cold coffee from Depaul's two doors down is the classic CP loop.

name: Depaul's
description: A hole-in-the-wall on Janpath that has sold one perfect thing since 1956: cold coffee in a glass bottle, frothed sweet and strong. The bottle-return ritual at the counter is part of the institution.
editor_note: Ask for less sugar if you must, but drink it standing in the Janpath crowd - that is the format.

name: Kake Da Hotel
description: A gloriously unreformed Punjabi dhaba on the Outer Circle, slinging butter chicken, keema and dal over shared tables since 1931. The decor is strip lights and steel plates; the gravy makes up for everything.
editor_note: Share a table with strangers, order the butter chicken with tandoori roti, and don't ask for a menu card.

name: Saravana Bhavan
description: The Janpath outpost of the Chennai institution, with a queue on the pavement at most mealtimes. Ghee roast dosas, mini-tiffin platters and filter coffee poured from a height - reliable as a metronome.
editor_note: The queue moves faster than it looks; hold out for the mini tiffin so you get a bit of everything.

name: Cafe Lota
description: Inside the National Crafts Museum complex, a bamboo-shaded courtyard cafe that quietly rewrote what Indian cafe food could be - sabudana popcorn, palak patta chaat and millet bowls drawn from regional home kitchens. Pair it with the museum's textile galleries.
editor_note: Order whatever fish dish is on that week and finish with the dark chocolate-stuffed gulab jamun.

name: Kitty Su
description: The Lalit's flagship club and one of India's few genuinely inclusive dance floors, with drag nights, international techno and house bookings, and a crowd that actually dances. Multiple rooms mean you can flee the main floor when it peaks.
editor_note: Their drag and pride nights are the best parties in the city - book the guest list ahead.

name: 24/7 Restaurant at The Lalit
description: The Lalit's round-the-clock coffee shop, the classic Delhi answer to post-club hunger at 4am - biryani, ramen and club sandwiches served under chandeliers while the city sleeps. Pricey, but it is literally always open.
editor_note: The 4am biryani after a Kitty Su night is a Delhi rite of passage.

name: Unplugged Courtyard
description: A sprawling open-air bar in CP's Inner Circle built around a real tree strung with fairy lights, with acoustic acts most evenings. The food is dependable North Indian-meets-bar-bites; the draw is drinking under the open sky in the middle of CP.
editor_note: Reserve a courtyard table just before sunset and stay through the first live set.

name: The Big Chill Cafe
description: The movie-poster-plastered Khan Market institution that taught Delhi to love penne alfredo and mud pie in equal measure. Portions are enormous, the queue is eternal, and the dessert fridge has broken more diets than any place in town.
editor_note: Don't leave without the Mississippi mud pie, even if you have to take it to a Lodhi Garden bench.

name: Bahrisons Booksellers
description: Founded in 1953 by a refugee from Rawalpindi, this is Delhi's most loved bookshop - floor-to-ceiling shelves, staff who actually read, and a front-of-store table that sets the city's reading agenda. The kids' annexe nearby is just as good.
editor_note: Tell the staff the last book you loved and let them pick your next one - they're never wrong.

name: Khan Chacha
description: The kebab-roll counter that started in a Khan Market alley in 1972 and became shorthand for the rumali roll itself. Chicken tikka and mutton seekh wrapped with onion rings and chutney, eaten standing in the back lane.
editor_note: Mutton seekh roll, extra chutney, eaten in the middle lane while you window-shop - accept no substitutes.

name: Cafe Turtle
description: Perched above the Full Circle bookstore, a sunny top-floor cafe with mismatched colours, herbal teas, mezze platters and serious cakes. The kind of place where you climb up with a new book and lose two hours.
editor_note: Buy downstairs, read upstairs - and the banoffee pie with fresh mint tea is the house ritual.

name: Perch Wine & Coffee Bar
description: A pale, Scandinavian-quiet room doing double duty: precise pour-overs by day, a sharp wine list and small plates by night. The truffle croque and a glass of riesling is a complete Khan Market evening.
editor_note: Go at the 5pm changeover when the coffee crowd thins and the wine crowd hasn't arrived.

name: Gulati, Pandara Road
description: Anchor of the Pandara Road market, the strip of North Indian restaurants that has fed post-wedding and post-party Delhi since the 1960s. Butter chicken, dal Gulati and burra kebabs served fast, rich and unapologetic until well past midnight.
editor_note: Pandara Road at 1am, butter chicken with garlic naan, is the city's most reliable celebration.

name: Have More, Pandara Road
description: Gulati's eternal next-door rival, with partisans who will argue its dal makhani is the truer article. Same late hours, same gleaming gravies, slightly shorter queue - which is sometimes the whole decision.
editor_note: When Gulati's wait crosses thirty minutes, walk two doors down and lose nothing.

name: National Gallery of Modern Art
description: The country's flagship modern art museum in Jaipur House near India Gate - Amrita Sher-Gil, the Bengal School, Raza and Souza across echoing colonial halls and a sculpture garden. Quiet on weekdays to the point of feeling private.
editor_note: Head straight to the Amrita Sher-Gil rooms first, before the school groups land.

name: Summer House Cafe
description: The first-floor terrace bar above Aurobindo Place market that has hosted half of India's indie circuit on its tiny stage. Gig nights are sweaty and joyful; off nights it's a loose, fairy-lit terrace hang that runs late.
editor_note: Check their gig calendar - a weeknight show here beats most weekend clubbing in town.

name: Hauz Khas Social
description: The original Social, stacked down the side of Hauz Khas Village with windows over the lake and deer park. Laptops and cold brew by day, LIITs in jam jars and a roaring crowd by night - the village's most dependable constant.
editor_note: Come at 4pm for the lake-view window table and simply never leave.

name: The Toddy Shop
description: A Kerala kallu-shaap homage up a Hauz Khas Village staircase - beef fry, Kuttanadan duck, kappa and meen curry served on enamel plates under matinee posters of Malayalam cinema. Loud, homey and gloriously unfussy.
editor_note: Order the beef fry with Kerala parotta and thank whoever brought you here later.

name: Kunzum Travel Cafe
description: The pay-what-you-like travel cafe and bookshop that became a clubhouse for Delhi's wanderers - travel talks, photography walls, self-serve coffee and shelves of guidebooks and travelogues. More community room than commerce.
editor_note: Drop in for one chai, stay for the travel-stories evening, leave with three new trip plans.

name: auro kitchen & bar
description: A leafy Aurobindo Marg bungalow that flips from Mediterranean dinner garden to one of Delhi's best small electronic-music floors after dark. The booking policy keeps the dance floor crowd genuinely music-first.
editor_note: Their Sunday evening listening sessions in the garden are the gentlest way to end a weekend.

name: Deer Park
description: The wooded park stitched between Hauz Khas Village and Safdarjung Enclave, with spotted deer in their enclosure, peacocks at large, and running trails that link to the medieval lake. The village's green lung and decompression chamber.
editor_note: Enter from the village side at golden hour and loop the lake before dinner.

name: Hauz Khas Fort & Lake
description: Firoz Shah's 14th-century madrasa and tomb stepping down to the royal tank, now Delhi's favourite sunset ledge. Students, couples and sketchbook-carriers line the stone windows as parakeets cross the water.
editor_note: The arched windows on the lake side are the seats - claim one an hour before sunset.

name: Coast Cafe
description: A calm, white-walled room above the village bustle doing coastal South Indian properly - Malabar fish curry, appams, Coorg pandi curry and a quietly excellent cocktail list. The antidote to the street below.
editor_note: Appams with the stew arrive faster than your climb up three floors deserves.

name: Naivedyam
description: A dim, temple-dark South Indian stalwart at the mouth of Hauz Khas Village, serving rasam in steel tumblers as a free opener before crisp rava dosas and proper filter coffee. Unmoved by every trend that has swept the village around it.
editor_note: The complimentary rasam shot is the best thing you'll drink in the village - dosas are a bonus.

name: Potbelly Rooftop Cafe
description: A rooftop perch above Shahpur Jat's tangle, serving Bihari food that's nearly impossible to find elsewhere in Delhi - litti chokha, champaran mutton, sattu sharbat. The view over the urban village's terraces is half the charm.
editor_note: Litti chokha and a sattu cooler at sunset on this roof is the correct order of operations.

name: Flipside Cafe
description: A pocket-sized specialty coffee bar in a Shahpur Jat lane, all blond wood and a counter you can barely turn around at. Single-origin pour-overs, proper flat whites and bake-of-the-day; the baristas remember your order by visit two.
editor_note: It seats about eight people, so go odd hours and let the barista choose your beans.

name: Greenr Cafe
description: A plant-filled, plant-forward cafe that made vegetarian and vegan eating feel easy rather than earnest - smoothie bowls, jackfruit tacos, oat-milk everything. Laptop-friendly without being a co-working farm.
editor_note: The shiitake bao and a cold brew on the upstairs seats is the regulars' order.

name: Dada Jungi House Lane
description: Shahpur Jat's designer spine - a medieval-village lane where wedding ateliers, sneaker murals and indie studios share walls with buffalo sheds and old Jat havelis. Window-shopping here is an architecture-and-street-art crawl in one.
editor_note: Look up as much as you look in shop windows - the best murals are a floor above eye level.

name: Blue Tokai Coffee Roasters, Champa Gali
description: One of the roastery's earliest and most loved outposts, at the end of Champa Gali's lane with the roasting machines visible behind glass. Estate-traceable pour-overs, excellent croissants, and a courtyard that smells of fresh roast all day.
editor_note: Order the seasonal estate as a pour-over and watch the roaster run a batch.

name: Jugmug Thela
description: The chai laboratory that anchors Champa Gali - single-origin teas, house masala blends and the famous All India Pass chai flight, with banana bread on the side. Started as a cart, now a pilgrimage for the city's tea nerds.
editor_note: On a rainy afternoon, the kulhad masala chai here is the single best seat in South Delhi.

name: Champa Gali Lane
description: A former dairy-and-carpentry lane in Saidulajab reborn as Delhi's most photogenic alley - fairy lights, studio-boutiques, pottery, and a string of small cafes between whitewashed walls. Best wandered slowly with no agenda.
editor_note: Weekday mornings it's still a sleepy village lane; weekends after 5pm it's a festival - pick your mood.

name: Devans South Indian Coffee & Tea
description: A Khanna Market roaster from 1962 that was third-wave before the term existed - they roast and grind estate beans at the counter and pull a filter coffee that puts most flat whites to shame. Take home a half-kilo of the house blend.
editor_note: Buy the peaberry, ask them to grind it coarse, and drink a filter coffee at the bench while you wait.

name: Lodhi Art District
description: India's first open-air public art district - dozens of giant murals by Indian and international artists across the whitewashed walls of Lodhi Colony's CPWD blocks. A self-guided walk between Khanna Market and Meharchand Market.
editor_note: Walk it early Sunday morning when the avenues are empty and the light hits the east-facing walls.

name: Lodhi Garden
description: Ninety acres of lawns and 15th-century Lodi and Sayyid tombs, where power-walking bureaucrats, courting couples and yoga groups share paths under some of Delhi's oldest trees. The Bara Gumbad at golden hour is the city's screensaver.
editor_note: Enter from the Athpula bridge side at 6am in winter - mist on the tombs, and you'll never go back to gyms.

name: Jamun
description: A jamun-purple dining room in Meharchand Market doing homestyle regional Indian with polish - Banarasi tamatar chaat, Andhra chicken, daulat ki chaat in winter. The cooking tastes like someone's grandmother got a tasting menu budget.
editor_note: If daulat ki chaat is on the menu, order it before they run out - it doesn't survive past evening.

name: India Habitat Centre - Visual Arts Gallery
description: The exhibition spaces inside Stein's red-brick Habitat Centre, with rotating photography and contemporary art shows, film screenings at Stein Auditorium and the plaza's famous blue-louvre canopy overhead. Free, central, and always showing something.
editor_note: Check the evening film or talk listings - the gallery-plus-screening double bill is Delhi's best free date.

name: Indian Accent
description: The restaurant that put modern Indian fine dining on the world map, now at The Lodhi hotel - blue cheese naan, daulat ki chaat, and a tasting menu that rethinks nostalgia course by course. Still the city's definitive special-occasion table.
editor_note: Book weeks ahead and do the full tasting with the non-alcoholic pairing - it's the kitchen at full stretch.

name: Mehrauli Archaeological Park
description: A hundred acres of scrub forest scattered with a millennium of ruins - Jamali Kamali mosque, Rajon ki Baoli stepwell, Balban's tomb - in the shadow of the Qutub Minar. Delhi's deepest history with almost no crowds.
editor_note: Start at Jamali Kamali, end at Rajon ki Baoli, and go before 9am when it's only birdsong and joggers.

name: Dramz Whiskey Bar & Lounge
description: A whisky library and terrace bar whose USP is unanswerable: a floodlit, eye-level view of the Qutub Minar over your old fashioned. Hundreds of whiskies, low jazz, and the best monument-gazing real estate in the city.
editor_note: Book the upper terrace edge table at dusk - the Minar lights come on around 7pm and the terrace goes quiet.

name: Olive Bar & Kitchen
description: The whitewashed, pebble-courtyard Mediterranean restaurant under a giant banyan in One Style Mile that has hosted two decades of Delhi's long lunches. Wood-fired pizzas, burrata and a Sunday brunch that is a social institution.
editor_note: Ask for a table under the banyan, not indoors - that tree is the whole point of Olive.

name: The Grammar Room
description: An airy, verandah-style all-day cafe behind Olive, with rattan chairs, a gravel garden and a menu of bowls, benedicts and very good coffee. South Delhi's favourite slow-breakfast spot, dogs welcome.
editor_note: Weekday breakfast on the verandah before 10am - after that, the brunch wave arrives with its labradors.

name: Depot48
description: The GK-2 listening room and bistro that gave Delhi's blues, folk and jazz acts a proper stage and a crowd that actually hushed for the sets. Vinyl on the walls, bourbon-friendly bar, songwriter nights that felt like someone's living room.
editor_note: Sit at the bar end near the stage and tip the band - this room runs on regulars who care.

name: Sidecar
description: A neighbourhood bar in GK-2 that climbed the World's 50 Best Bars list without losing its records-and-bar-stools soul. Classics done perfectly, a rotating menu of originals, vinyl spinning, and bartenders who remember faces.
editor_note: Sit at the counter, tell them what you last loved drinking, and surrender the menu.

name: Fig & Maple
description: Chef Radhika Khandelwal's rooftop kitchen in GK-2, championing zero-waste cooking and hyperlocal produce before it was fashionable - beetroot-greens pestos, all-day brunch plates and an ingredient-led menu that changes with the mandi.
editor_note: Trust the specials board over the menu - that's where the morning's market haul ends up.

name: Diva
description: Ritu Dalmia's M-block GK-2 Italian, feeding the neighbourhood handmade pasta and serious wine since 2000 - long before Delhi had an Italian scene to speak of. White tablecloths without stiffness; the tasting menus still surprise.
editor_note: The off-menu burrata course exists if you ask nicely, and lunch prix fixe is the value play.

name: Kiran Nadar Museum of Art
description: India's foremost private museum of modern and contemporary art, improbably housed in a Saket mall - Raza, Husain, Nasreen Mohamedi and ambitious contemporary retrospectives, free to enter. World-class curation, zero queue.
editor_note: It's free and empty on weekday afternoons - the best-kept cultural secret in a city of monuments.

name: Mahabelly
description: The Kerala restaurant that made appam-and-toddy-shop food a destination in a Saket mall plaza - fiery Kuttanadan duck, prawn moilee, beef ularthiyathu and Malabar parottas pulled apart at the table. Loud, generous and reliably packed.
editor_note: Order the appams with mutton stew first and decide the rest of the meal after - everyone does.

name: Rose Cafe
description: A pastel, vintage-furnished cottage cafe on Westend Marg near the Champa Gali turn-off, beloved for quiches, lemon tarts and pots of tea on rose-printed china. Feels airlifted from a hill station.
editor_note: The veranda table at tea-time with the lemon tart is the move; weekdays only if you want quiet.

name: PCO
description: Delhi's original speakeasy - a rotary-phone door code, a dim Vasant Vihar basement, and cocktails that kicked off the city's modern bar movement. The classics programme and bartender bench remain among India's best.
editor_note: Get the week's code from a member or the reservation line, and start with whatever their bartender's choice is.

name: Cafe Delhi Heights
description: The dependable all-day crowd-pleaser at the Vasant Kunj malls, home of the famous Juicy Lucy burger and a menu that runs from khao suey to dim sum without embarrassment. Where South-West Delhi actually eats between movies.
editor_note: It's the Juicy Lucy or nothing - everything else on the menu is for the second visit.

name: Roshan Di Kulfi
description: The Ajmal Khan Road institution that has paired chole bhature with kulfi faluda since 1948 - an objectively unhinged combination that all of Karol Bagh swears by. The kesar kulfi, dense and saffron-deep, is the point.
editor_note: Do the full ritual: chole bhature first, kulfi faluda after, regret nothing.

name: May Day Bookstore & Cafe
description: LeftWord's radical bookshop near Shadipur, stacked with political theory, translations and small-press titles you will not find in mall bookstores, plus chai and the occasional reading or film night. A bookshop with convictions.
editor_note: Their May Day anniversary sale is legendary - and the staff recommendations skew brilliant and unsparing.

name: Ashok & Ashok Meat Dhaba
description: A near-mythical Sadar Bazar-side dhaba that cooks one cauldron of meat masala and a pot of chicken a day, sells out by mid-afternoon, and closes. The mutton korma, slicked with red oil and eaten with roghni roti, has a cult that arrives before noon.
editor_note: Land by 12:30pm or you are eating somewhere else - there are no second batches.

name: Gaffar Market
description: Karol Bagh's grey-market bazaar of phones, gadgets, imported chocolate and everything in between, running shoulder-to-shoulder since long before e-commerce. Even if you buy nothing, the haggling theatre is worth the trip.
editor_note: Quote half the asking price, walk away once, and check everything works before you leave the stall.

name: Moolchand Parathewala
description: The all-night paratha stand under the Moolchand flyover where club crowds, cab drivers and surgeons from nearby hospitals converge at 3am for anda and aloo-pyaaz parathas off the tawa, with chai in kulhads. Delhi's great social equalizer.
editor_note: The egg paratha with the green chutney at 3am tastes better than anything you ate at dinner.

name: Lajpat Nagar Central Market
description: The great middle-class bazaar of South Delhi - mehendi-wallahs, fabric shops, wedding lehengas, ram laddoo carts and a soundtrack of a thousand negotiations. Come for kurtas, stay for the chaat-and-chaos circuit.
editor_note: Get mehendi done on a weekday evening and eat ram laddoos while it dries - that's the full Lajpat experience.

name: Dolma Aunty Momos
description: Dolma Tsering set up her steamer in Lajpat Nagar in 1994 and effectively taught Delhi to eat momos. The steamed chicken momos with the incendiary red chutney remain the benchmark every street stall is measured against.
editor_note: One plate is never enough, and the chutney-to-momo ratio is a personality test.

name: Kabul Delhi Restaurant
description: In the heart of Lajpat Nagar's Afghan quarter, a no-frills dining hall serving Kabuli pulao heaped with raisins and carrots, lamb kebabs and fresh naan-e-Afghani from the tandoor next door. The bakeries on this stretch alone justify the trip.
editor_note: Buy a sheet of warm Afghan naan from the bakery outside on your way out - it barely survives the walk to the car.

story.caption: Thursday evening. The qawwals tune up as the dargah fills with regulars.
Sit on the marble, leave your shoes at the gate, let the harmonium start.
Stay past the first song. The room opens up somewhere in the second.

name: Hazrat Nizamuddin Dargah Qawwali
description: The 14th-century Sufi shrine where qawwals have sung in the marble courtyard for seven centuries, loudest and most transporting on Thursday evenings after the maghrib prayer. Rose petals, incense, and music that dissolves whoever you were when you walked in.
editor_note: Go Thursday just before sunset, leave your shoes at a shop you'll remember, and sit through at least three qawwalis.

name: Sunder Nursery
description: A 90-acre Mughal-era nursery restored into Delhi's most beautiful park - Persian-style water channels, Unesco-listed tombs, a lake, micro-forests and Sunday farmers' markets. Picnic culture found its capital here.
editor_note: Sunday morning: farmers' market first, then a picnic rug under the big amaltas near Sunder Burj.

story.caption: The first garden-tomb on the subcontinent — the blueprint the Taj would borrow.
Come at opening. The lawns are empty, the light is low, and the dome glows.
Walk the char-bagh quarters out to the edges most visitors never reach.

name: Humayun's Tomb
description: The red sandstone precursor to the Taj, sitting in a perfect charbagh garden that glows at first and last light. Restored to almost uncanny beauty; the side gardens and Isa Khan's octagonal tomb are quieter than the main axis.
editor_note: Enter at opening time and walk to Isa Khan's enclosure first - you'll have a 16th-century garden to yourself.

name: Ghalib Kabab Corner
description: A smoke-wreathed kebab counter in the Nizamuddin basti lanes, grilling buttery seekh and tikka over coals for the dargah crowd. Eaten on the spot with rumali roti and onions, ideally after Thursday qawwali.
editor_note: Post-qawwali seekh kebabs in the lane is the Thursday-night double feature locals never skip.

name: Comesum, Nizamuddin Railway Station
description: The 24-hour food hall outside Hazrat Nizamuddin station - dosas, biryani, chowmein and gulab jamun under tube lights at any hour, surrounded by train travellers and 4am stragglers. Not fancy, eternally open.
editor_note: It's nobody's favourite restaurant and everybody's 4am salvation - the dosa is the safest bet.

name: AMA Cafe
description: The multi-level cafe at the heart of the Tibetan colony, famous for towering breakfast plates, blueberry pancakes, and bottomless ginger-lemon-honey tea. Students nurse a single americano here for entire afternoons and no one minds.
editor_note: Order the pancakes and the ginger-honey-lemon even if it's 4pm - breakfast rules don't apply in MT.

name: Tee Dee Restaurant
description: An MT old-guard canteen where Tibetan families actually eat - laphing slick with chilli oil, shabhaley, thenthuk and bowls of thukpa that fix most of what's wrong with you. Plastic stools, fast turnover, deep comfort.
editor_note: Cold laphing to start, mutton thenthuk to finish - and go off-peak or you're queuing on the stairs.

name: Rigo Restaurant
description: An MT favourite that straddles Tibetan and Korean comfort food - bibimbap, kimchi stew and ramyun alongside momos and shapta, reflecting the colony's student traffic. The rooftop seats catch the river breeze.
editor_note: The kimchi fried rice with a fried egg is the order the regulars won't admit to loving more than momos.

name: Yamuna Ghat at Sunrise
description: The riverbank ghats near Majnu ka Tilla where boatmen row you out at dawn through thousands of migratory seagulls in winter, mist on the water and the city invisible behind you. The most un-Delhi hour Delhi offers.
editor_note: Arrive by 6am November to February, pay the boatman fairly, and buy a bag of feed for the gulls.

name: Sita Ram Diwan Chand
description: The 1950s Paharganj shop that serves arguably Delhi's definitive chole bhature - fluffy paneer-flecked bhature with chickpeas simmered overnight, finished with pickled carrots and banta soda. One dish, done since Partition, still under a hundred rupees.
editor_note: Go before 11am; by noon the bhature lose the breakfast-crowd freshness that makes them transcendent.

name: Sam's Cafe
description: The rooftop cafe of the Vivek Hotel on Main Bazaar, a backpacker landmark with banana pancakes, Israeli platters, thalis and a view over Paharganj's rooftop tangle of wires and water tanks. The menu is a map of every traveller who passed through.
editor_note: Sunset on the roof with a banana lassi, watching the bazaar below, is peak Paharganj romance.

name: Main Bazaar, Paharganj
description: The backpacker bazaar opposite New Delhi station - incense, bootleg band t-shirts, brass buddhas, secondhand novels in six languages and juice stands, running late into the night. Scruffy, hustling, and weirdly lovable.
editor_note: The used-book stalls buy back what they sell you - Delhi's original circular economy.

name: Tadka 4986
description: A clean, honest vegetarian thali joint amid Main Bazaar's chaos, where backpackers and railway passengers alike get dal, seasonal sabzi and phulkas that taste of a home kitchen. The kind of place you remember on sick days abroad.
editor_note: The simple dal-chawal thali here has rescued more jet-lagged travellers than any pharmacy on the strip.

name: Ek Bar
description: A Defence Colony cocktail den that drinks like a love letter to India - paan-infused gins, chai-spiced old fashioneds and a riotous, art-deco-meets-truck-art interior. One of the first bars to take Indian ingredients behind the stick seriously.
editor_note: Order off the India-map cocktail menu by region and let the bartender pick your second round.

name: Sagar Ratna
description: The 1986 Defence Colony original that became North India's default South Indian restaurant - crisp paper dosas, idli-vada plates and filter coffee, served fast in a bright family-packed hall. The chain went everywhere; this branch stayed the benchmark.
editor_note: Sunday breakfast here is a Defence Colony tradition older than most of its diners - go before 10.

name: Swagath
description: Defence Colony market's coastal stalwart, doing Mangalorean and Chettinad seafood with conviction - butter-pepper-garlic crab, gassi with neer dosa, appam-stew. The dining room is dated and nobody cares; the crab is the decor.
editor_note: Bib up and order the butter-pepper-garlic crab with neer dosas - it's a two-hand commitment.

name: The Piano Man Jazz Club
description: The Safdarjung Enclave room that single-handedly built Delhi's jazz audience - a tiny double-height club with a grand piano, nightly live sets, and a strictly-listen crowd. Indian and touring acts, no cover most nights, drinks priced for the privilege.
editor_note: Arrive by 8 for a banquette near the stage, and don't talk during the sets - the room will turn on you.

name: Evergreen Sweet House
description: The Green Park halwai-institution since 1963 - bhature with amritsari chole downstairs, trays of ghee-bright badam barfi and gulab jamun at the counter, and South Delhi's most democratic breakfast crowd. Mithai boxes from here settle family debts.
editor_note: Weekend mornings, the chole bhature queue is the neighbourhood's real town square.

name: Dilli Haat, INA
description: The open-air crafts bazaar where state emporia meet state food stalls - Naga pork thali, Bihari litti, momos from the Sikkim stall, and handloom from weavers who rotate in fortnightly. A tour of India for a token entry fee.
editor_note: Skip the trinket lanes, eat across three state food stalls, and buy directly from the weaver-run stands at the back.

name: Sarojini Nagar Market
description: Delhi's legendary export-surplus clothing bazaar, where last season's international labels surface for the price of a coffee. Requires stamina, sharp elbows and a gift for spotting the one good piece in a pile of forty.
editor_note: Go Tuesday-to-Thursday morning with cash and an empty backpack; weekend Sarojini is a contact sport.

name: AIIMS Gate Night Chai Stalls
description: The cluster of tea-and-omelette carts outside AIIMS that never really close - serving night-shift doctors, anxious families and post-party stragglers the same cutting chai and bun-omelette at 3am. Delhi's most honest all-night counter.
editor_note: The 3am bun-omelette with adrak chai here has talked more people through hard nights than any bar in town.

name: Chache Di Hatti
description: The Kamla Nagar chole bhature counter that Delhi University students have sworn by since 1952 - small, fiery plates handed over a crowded counter, usually finished standing in the lane. It routinely sells out by mid-afternoon.
editor_note: Order two plates upfront; the queue is too long to rejoin once the first plate disappears.

name: Bille Di Hatti
description: Chache's eternal Kamla Nagar rival, backing its chole bhature with a sweet, malai-topped lassi in steel glasses. Generations of North Campus students have run their entire friendships on the Chache-versus-Bille debate.
editor_note: Whatever side of the chole war you're on, the lassi here is undisputed territory.

name: QD's Restaurant
description: The Kamla Nagar joint widely credited with inventing the tandoori momo - char-blistered, butter-slathered, rolled in masala and served with mint chutney to permanent crowds of DU students. Inauthentic to Tibet, essential to Delhi.
editor_note: It's the tandoori momos and a cold coffee, eaten on the hood of someone's scooter - that's the format.

name: Big Yellow Door
description: The DU-belt cafe with the eponymous yellow door, built for student budgets - loaded fries, freak shakes, pasta bowls and wall-doodles, with prices that let you stay all evening on one order. The unofficial common room of North Campus.
editor_note: Their pocket-money pricing is the whole point - order the BYD special shake and camp with your notes.

name: Food Exchange, Novotel Aerocity
description: The round-the-clock interactive kitchen at Novotel Aerocity - live counters, biryani, noodles and a breakfast spread that starts while the late-night crowd is still finishing dessert. The reliable answer when a red-eye flight meets real hunger.
editor_note: Between a 2am landing and a 6am meeting, this is the city's most civilized holding pattern.

name: Mr. Choy, Worldmark
description: A glossy Cantonese-style diner at Worldmark Aerocity doing dim sum, wontons and Hong Kong noodles deep into the night - one of the rare non-hotel kitchens near the airport still plating past 1am. Bright, quick and surprisingly good for the hour.
editor_note: The prawn wonton noodle soup at 1am before a red-eye is the frequent-flyer's secret handshake.

name: Toy Room
description: The London-import club at Aerocity with its mascot bear, hip-hop-heavy DJ sets and a crowd dressed for the cameras. Runs among the latest closing times in the city, which at 3am is the only review that matters.
editor_note: Get on the guest list and arrive after midnight - the room doesn't make sense before that.

name: Garam Dharam, Cyber Hub
description: A Murthal-style highway dhaba reimagined as Bollywood theatre at Cyber Hub, themed on Dharmendra films - truck-art booths, lassi in steel, amritsari kulchas and tandoori platters served late for the corporate-party crowd. Loud, silly, satisfying.
editor_note: It's the closest thing to a Murthal paratha run without leaving the city - go post-midnight when the suits loosen up.

name: Museo Camera Centre for the Photographic Arts
description: South Asia's largest crowd-funded photography museum, with thousands of vintage cameras, rotating exhibitions and darkroom workshops in a striking concrete shell near Sector 28. A pilgrimage for anyone who has ever loved film grain.
editor_note: Time your visit with one of their weekend darkroom or cyanotype workshops - they sell out quietly.

name: Whisky Samba
description: Two Horizon Center's grown-up whisky bar, with one of NCR's deepest single-malt walls, serious cocktails and a kitchen that outperforms most standalone restaurants. Where Gurgaon goes when it wants quiet money rather than loud music.
editor_note: Ask for the whisky flight with the bartender's commentary - it's the best malt education in NCR.

name: Brahmaputra Market, Sector 29
description: Noida's beloved old street-food strip - momos, chowmein, shawarma, chaat and chai stalls packed gully-to-gully with students and office crowds until late. Scrappier and better than the malls a kilometre away.
editor_note: The momo stalls at the back corner outsell everything for a reason - eat standing, repeat order immediately.

name: Atta Market, Sector 18
description: Noida's chaotic answer to Sarojini - export-surplus clothes, phone covers, jhumkas and street snacks crammed into lanes beside the Sector 18 towers. Bargaining is mandatory; finds are real.
editor_note: Hit the lanes behind the main drag - the front rows are tourist prices, the back rows are the real market.
